title: Probabilities you can trust
objectives: Check whether predicted probabilities are calibrated
Read a reliability diagram and compute the Brier score
Calibrate a model on held-out data

screens.prose: A $k$-nearest-neighbours model with $k = 3$ was fitted on 1,000 loans and scores 1,000 newer ones. On 48 loans all three neighbours had defaulted, so it said “default, probability 1”. Of those 48 loans, 33 defaulted.
screens.question: What fraction of the loans it was “certain” about actually defaulted?

hints.text: Divide the loans that defaulted by the loans it scored 1.
33 defaulted out of 48.

byKey.one: That is what the model said. Count what happened: 33 of 48.
byKey.rest: 0.3125 is the share that repaid. The question asks for the share that defaulted.

explain.text: A model that says 1 should be right every time; this one was right 69% of the time. A forecast is **calibrated** when its $p$ comes true a fraction $p$ of the times it is said.

screens.prose: One number for the whole diagram is the **Brier score**: the mean squared error of the probabilities, $\frac{1}{n}\sum (p_i - y_i)^2$. It is level 1's MSE with outcomes 0 and 1. Four loans:
screens.question: What is their Brier score?

hints.text: Square each gap between $p$ and $y$.
The gaps are 0.1, 0.2, 0.6 and 0.1.

feedback.generic: Not quite right. Average the squared gaps $(p_i - y_i)^2$.

byKey.sum: 0.42 is the sum. Divide by the 4 loans.
byKey.abs: 0.25 averages the gaps without squaring them.

explain.text: The one wrong-way call, 0.6 on a loan that repaid, supplies 0.36 of the 0.42. Lower is better: our logistic model scores 0.134 on the test loans, $k$-NN 0.177. Brier splits into a calibration part, minus a resolution part, plus the base rate's own uncertainty.

screens.prose: Here are $k$-NN's four bins as bars: what it said beside what happened. With $k = 3$ it can only say 0, 1/3, 2/3 or 1.
screens.question: Why are $k$-NN's probabilities so extreme with $k = 3$?

options.text: Each prediction is a vote of three noisy neighbours, so one unlucky neighbour moves it by a third
$k$-NN is biased towards predicting default
options.why: It errs both ways: too high on the right, too low on the left. That is spread, not a lean one way.

options.text: The features were not scaled
options.why: Scaling changes which loans are neighbours, but three votes can still only give four values.

options.text: 1,000 training loans are too few for any model
options.why: Logistic regression on the same loans is well calibrated.

hints.text: List the values three votes can give.
Three neighbours give 0, 1/3, 2/3 or 1, nothing in between.
A prediction from three noisy votes is high-variance, as small $k$ was in level 1: it overshoots both ways.

feedback.correct: Small $k$ means high variance, and high variance shows up as overconfidence.
feedback.generic: Not quite right. Ask what three votes can and cannot say.

explain.text: Three votes give coarse, noisy probabilities, so the extremes are often wrong. Larger $k$ smooths them; $k = 5$ already lowers the Brier score from 0.177 to 0.160. Calibration can also be repaired afterwards, as we see next.

screens.prose: Model C ignores the features and says 0.233, the training default rate, for every loan. On the 1,000 test loans 23.9% defaulted. Its Brier score is 0.182.
screens.question: How should we judge model C?

options.text: Almost perfectly calibrated, and useless: AUC 0.5, so it cannot tell loans apart
The best model: its one bin sits on the diagonal
options.why: Calibration alone is easy. Saying the base rate every time is calibrated and tells you nothing about any loan.

options.text: Badly calibrated, since it never says 0 or 1
options.why: Calibration asks whether 0.233 comes true 23.3% of the time. It does, nearly: 23.9%.

options.text: Good: its AUC is 1, since it never ranks a pair wrongly
options.why: Every pair is a tie, and ties count half: AUC 0.5.

hints.text: Plot C's single bin on the reliability diagram.
One dot at (0.233, 0.239): almost on the diagonal.
Every pair of loans ties, so AUC is 0.5. Brier 0.182 is worse than logistic's 0.134.

feedback.correct: Calibration is necessary, not enough: a forecast must also separate the loans.
feedback.generic: Not quite right. Check C's calibration and its ranking separately.

explain.text: C sits on the diagonal and ranks nothing. Brier rewards both calibration and resolution, so C's 0.182 loses to logistic's 0.134. Good models are calibrated and sharp.

widget.solution:
from sklearn.neighbors import KNeighborsClassifier
from sklearn.calibration import CalibratedClassifierCV

def calibrated_knn(X_train, y_train, X_test):
    base = KNeighborsClassifier(n_neighbors=5)
    model = CalibratedClassifierCV(base, method='isotonic', cv=5)
    model.fit(X_train, y_train)
    probs = model.predict_proba(X_test)[:, 1]
    return [round(float(v), 4) for v in probs]

rng = np.random.default_rng(21)
n = 2000
lev = np.round(rng.uniform(0.5, 7.5, n), 2)

widget.solution:
def reliability_bins(y, p, n_bins):
    # bin i holds p in [i/n_bins, (i+1)/n_bins); p = 1 goes in the last bin
    # return [(mean p, observed frequency, count), ...] for non-empty bins, rounded to 4
    groups = [[] for _ in range(n_bins)]
    for yi, pi in zip(y, p):
        i = min(int(pi * n_bins), n_bins - 1)
        groups[i].append((yi, pi))
    out = []
    for g in groups:
        if g:
            mean_p = sum(pi for _, pi in g) / len(g)
            freq = sum(yi for yi, _ in g) / len(g)
            out.append((round(mean_p, 4), round(freq, 4), len(g)))
    return out

screens.prose: You take even-money bets that truly win with probability 0.55. The Kelly rule from the conditional course stakes $2p - 1$ of capital. An overconfident model says 0.65, so it stakes 0.30 instead of 0.10. Growth per bet is $$G(f) = 0.55\ln(1 + f) + 0.45\ln(1 - f).$$
screens.question: What is $G(0.30)$, the growth per bet when you follow the overconfident model? Give 4 decimal places.

hints.text: Put $f = 0.30$ into $G$.

feedback.generic: Not quite right. Use the true 0.55 and the stake 0.30.

byKey.cal: 0.0050 is $G(0.10)$, the calibrated stake. The overconfident model stakes 0.30.
byKey.model-p: You used the model's 0.65 as the true chance. The bets really win 55% of the time.
byKey.sign: 0.55 ln 1.3 is 0.1443 and 0.45 ln 0.7 is −0.1605, so the loss term is the bigger. A positive 0.0162 books the shrinking capital as growth.

explain.text: Staking 0.30 loses about 1.6% per bet in the long run; staking 0.10 grows 0.5%. The same ranking, sized by an overconfident probability, turns an edge into ruin. Sizing needs calibration; AUC is not enough.

ideas: A calibrated model's 0.8 comes true 80% of the time. A reliability diagram shows this bin by bin against the diagonal.
Brier is the MSE of the probabilities; ECE averages each bin's gap. Both are judged on held-out data.
AUC sees only the ranking: a cubed model ranks as well and is badly calibrated, and position sizing needs calibration.

quiz.question: What goes wrong?

Nothing: more data for calibration is better
options.why: $k$-NN memorised these loans. Its scores on them are not what it will give new loans.

options.text: It is slow, but the result is the same
options.why: The result differs. New loans get mapped as if the model were as sure as on loans it has seen.

options.text: It lowers the model's AUC
options.why: Isotonic maps are rising, so they barely change the ranking. The damage is to the probabilities.

feedback.generic: Not quite right. Ask how $k$-NN scores a loan it was fitted on.
